---
title: "How Self-Attention Moves Information"
subtitle: "Queries, keys, values, causal masking, and where attention sits inside a transformer block"
---

*Prerequisites: comfort with vectors as lists of numbers and with the
idea of a weighted sum. `learn/why-transformers.qmd` explains why this
mechanism was wanted; `learn/tokens-context.qmd` explains where the input
vectors come from. Neither is assumed, and each is linked where it
matters.*

## 1. Why information has to move

Every token enters a transformer as a vector looked up from a table by
its token ID. The same token begins from the same learned token
embedding wherever it occurs; its later representation can differ
because of context, and the representation that is useful for predicting
what comes next depends on the surrounding text. Something inside the
network has to let the vector at one position be updated using the
vectors at other positions. Self-attention is that mechanism.

Take the sentence fragment

> "The bridge was closed because it"

and consider predicting the next token. Whatever the network predicts, a
good prediction needs to know what "it" refers to, and that information
sits at the position of ` bridge`, several positions earlier. In an
autoregressive language model, the kind this course is about, the
prediction at a position may use that position and the ones before it,
never the ones after. So the mechanism has to let the representation at
the position of "it" draw on earlier positions, and it has to do so
without any hand-written rule saying that pronouns look for nouns. It is
learned, like everything else in the network.

## 2. One attention head, conceptually

Fix one position $i$, the destination, whose representation is about to
be updated. The permitted source positions are $i$ itself and every
earlier position. A single **attention head** does the following with the
vectors at those positions.

First, three learned transformations are applied. The vector at the
destination is transformed into a **query** vector $\mathbf{q}_i$. The
vector at each permitted source position $j$ is transformed into a
**key** vector $\mathbf{k}_j$ and, separately, into a **value** vector
$\mathbf{v}_j$. All three are ordinary matrix multiplications with
matrices the network learned during training; there is nothing else
inside them.

Second, the query is compared with each key. The comparison is a dot
product, a single number for each pair $(i, j)$, and it serves as a
compatibility score. The dot product is large and positive when the two
vectors are strongly aligned, and its value depends on both their
alignment and their magnitudes.

Third, the scores over the permitted source positions are turned into
weights that are nonnegative and sum to one. The function that does this
is softmax, the same one that turns output scores into next-token
probabilities in `learn/softmax-sampling.qmd`; here it is applied across
positions rather than across the vocabulary.

Fourth, the head returns to position $i$ a weighted sum of the value
vectors, each value weighted by its attention weight. A source position
with a large weight contributes most of its value vector; one with a
tiny weight contributes almost nothing. That weighted sum is the
information moved to position $i$ in this head at this layer. [S-36]

Why three separate transformations, and why these names? The
architecture separates *what is compared* (query against key) from
*what is transferred* (the value), so that the network can learn to
match positions on one basis and transfer information on another. The
names come from that division of labor. As a way of holding the
mechanism in mind, it can help to read the query as "what the
destination is looking for" and the key as "what the source offers".
That reading is an intuition for learned vector matching and nothing
more: a query is a projected vector, not a question, and nothing in the
network assigns it a meaning a person could read off.

## 3. The mathematics

Write $\mathbf{x}_i$ for the incoming representation at position $i$,
the vector that arrives at this layer (at the first layer, the token's
initial representation after whatever positional mechanism the
architecture uses; at later layers, the output of the previous block).
For one head, the three transformations are

$$
\mathbf{q}_i = W_Q \mathbf{x}_i, \qquad
\mathbf{k}_j = W_K \mathbf{x}_j, \qquad
\mathbf{v}_j = W_V \mathbf{x}_j
$$

where $W_Q$, $W_K$, and $W_V$ are the head's learned parameter matrices.
The queries and keys have the same length, written $d_k$; the values may
have a different length. The compatibility score between destination $i$
and source $j$ is the dot product of query and key, divided by the square
root of $d_k$:

$$
s_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{q}_i^{\top} \mathbf{k}_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}
$$

Applying softmax across the permitted source positions turns the scores
into attention weights:

$$
a_{ij} = \frac{\exp(s_{ij})}{\sum_{j'} \exp(s_{ij'})}
$$

where the sum in the denominator runs over the permitted sources $j'$ for
destination $i$. Every $a_{ij}$ is positive and, for each $i$, the weights
sum to one. The head's output at position $i$ is the weighted sum of the
values:

$$
\mathbf{y}_i = \sum_{j} a_{ij}\, \mathbf{v}_j
$$

This is scaled dot-product attention, as the original Transformer paper
defined it: compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide
each by $\sqrt{d_k}$, apply softmax to obtain the weights on the values.
[S-36]

The division by $\sqrt{d_k}$ is there for a practical reason. A dot
product adds up $d_k$ terms, so as $d_k$ grows the scores tend to grow in
magnitude. Large scores push softmax toward putting almost all its weight
on one position, and in that regime the gradients that training relies
on become very small. The paper's authors state exactly this concern and
scale the dot products by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ to counteract it. [S-36] For
this page it is enough to know that the scaling keeps the scores in a
range where softmax remains sensitive to differences between them.

## 4. Causal masking

In an autoregressive decoder, position $i$ may attend to itself and to
earlier positions, and not to later ones. The way this is enforced is
simple: before softmax, the scores $s_{ij}$ for every future position
$j > i$ are replaced by a value so negative that $\exp$ of it is
effectively zero, so those positions receive zero weight and the
remaining weights still sum to one over the permitted positions. [S-22]

This matters most during training. The whole training sequence is
present at once, so the network could in principle look at the token it
is supposed to predict. The mask prevents that: the prediction at
position $i$ is computed from positions $1$ to $i$ only, exactly as it
would be at generation time when the later tokens do not yet exist.
`learn/training.qmd` explains what that makes possible, namely
evaluating the predictions for every position of a sequence in one
forward pass.

Not every transformer uses this mask. An encoder, such as the one in the
original Transformer's machine-translation model or in BERT, uses
bidirectional self-attention in which every position may attend to every
other, because its job is to represent a complete input rather than to
generate it token by token. [S-22] [S-24] When this course says
"self-attention" without qualification, it means the causal, decoder
form.

## 5. A small numerical example

Take the first three tokens of the running sentence, one attention head,
and vectors of length $d_k = d_v = 2$, so that every number can be
followed by hand. Suppose the three learned transformations have already
been applied to the incoming representations and produced the following
query, key, and value vectors. The numbers are invented for illustration.

<!-- check:qkv -->

| Position | Token | $\mathbf{q}$ | $\mathbf{k}$ | $\mathbf{v}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `The` | (1, 0) | (1, 0) | (2, 0) |
| 2 | ` bridge` | (0, 2) | (0, 1) | (0, 2) |
| 3 | ` was` | (2, 1) | (1, 1) | (1, 1) |

Scores are dot products divided by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$. With the
causal mask, position 1 may attend only to itself, position 2 to
positions 1 and 2, and position 3 to all three. Masked entries are shown
as "—".

<!-- check:scores -->

| Destination $i$ | $s_{i1}$ | $s_{i2}$ | $s_{i3}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.707 | — | — |
| 2 | 0.000 | 1.414 | — |
| 3 | 1.414 | 0.707 | 2.121 |

For position 3, for example, $s_{31} = (2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0)/1.414 =
1.414$, $s_{32} = (2 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1)/1.414 = 0.707$, and $s_{33} =
(2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1)/1.414 = 2.121$. Softmax across each row's
permitted entries gives the attention weights:

<!-- check:weights -->

| Destination $i$ | $a_{i1}$ | $a_{i2}$ | $a_{i3}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.000 | — | — |
| 2 | 0.196 | 0.804 | — |
| 3 | 0.284 | 0.140 | 0.576 |

Each row sums to one. Position 1 has only itself to attend to, so its
weight is 1 regardless of its score. Finally, each destination receives
the weighted sum of the value vectors of its permitted sources:

<!-- check:outputs -->

| Destination $i$ | $\mathbf{y}_i$ |
|---|---|
| 1 | (2.000, 0.000) |
| 2 | (0.391, 1.609) |
| 3 | (1.144, 0.856) |

For position 3: $0.284 \cdot (2, 0) + 0.140 \cdot (0, 2) + 0.576 \cdot
(1, 1) = (1.144, 0.856)$. The three permitted sources contribute
different amounts: most of the update comes from position 3's own value,
a substantial share from position 1, and little from position 2. Change
the query at position 3 and the weights change; change a key and the
weights for every destination that can see it change. In a trained model
those vectors were all produced by learned matrices from the incoming
representations, so the pattern of weights is itself something training
shaped. Every number above is recomputed by
`scripts/check_attention_example.py`.

## 6. Multi-head attention

One head produces one pattern of weights per destination. A transformer
layer runs several heads in parallel, each with its own $W_Q$, $W_K$,
and $W_V$, so that several attention patterns can operate at once over
the same positions. The heads' outputs are concatenated and passed
through one more learned matrix to produce the layer's attention output.
The original Transformer used eight heads, each working with query, key,
and value vectors of length 64, and described the purpose as letting the
model "jointly attend to information from different representation
subspaces at different positions." [S-37]

That is the whole claim. It is tempting to go further and say that one
head handles grammar, another handles names, and so on. The architecture
does not assign each head a fixed human-readable job, and the training
objective does not either, so a reader should not assume that a head
corresponds to a stable concept such as grammar, names, or topics without
separate evidence. [S-45]

## 7. Attention is one part of a transformer block

Self-attention is not the transformer. It is one of two main
computations inside each repeating block, and a model stacks many such
blocks. The hierarchy runs:

- a language model, the trained function as a whole;
- its transformer architecture;
- the repeated transformer blocks that make up most of it;
- inside each block, an attention mechanism and a feed-forward
  computation.

Attention, as above, exchanges information between positions. The
**feed-forward** (or MLP) sublayer does the other kind of work: it is
applied to each position separately and identically, with no exchange
between positions, and in the original design consists of two linear
transformations with a nonlinearity between them, the same
weighted-sum-then-nonlinearity pattern that `learn/neural-networks.qmd`
works through on a single unit. [S-38] [S-19] After attention has
gathered information from other positions into position $i$, the
feed-forward sublayer computes on that gathered vector alone.

Two further ingredients hold the block together. A **residual
connection** adds each sublayer's input to its output, so that a sublayer
computes an update to the representation rather than a replacement for
it. **Normalization** rescales the vectors so that their values stay in a
workable range through many layers. In the original Transformer, each
sublayer's output was the normalization of the residual sum, written
$\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))$. [S-38] Many later decoder
architectures use a different arrangement; GPT-2, for instance, moved the
normalization to the input of each sublayer. [S-39] The exact ordering is
a property of the named architecture, not of transformers in general,
and this page does not fix one.

## 8. What attention weights do and do not mean

The weights $a_{ij}$ determine how the value vectors are combined inside
one head, at one layer, for one destination. That is a precise, local
role. It is a mistake to read more into them. A large weight from
position $i$ to position $j$ is not a probability that token $j$ caused
token $i$, and an attention weight describes one local weighted
combination inside one head and layer; it is not by itself a complete
explanation of the model's final output, which depends on every head in
every layer, on the feed-forward sublayers, and on the residual stream
carrying earlier representations forward. Attention weights are a useful
window into one step of the computation, and only that. [S-45]

## 9. The cost of comparing every pair

Because each destination computes a score against every permitted source,
one layer of dense self-attention performs a number of comparisons that
grows with the square of the sequence length. That is the source of the
$O(n^2 \cdot d)$ arithmetic cost per layer that `learn/why-transformers.qmd`
discusses, together with what it does and does not imply. [S-17] This
page adds only the mechanism behind the count: the comparisons are the
dot products $\mathbf{q}_i^{\top}\mathbf{k}_j$ of §3, one per pair.

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>In one head, what is compared with what, and what is actually
transferred to the destination position?</summary>
The destination's query vector is compared, by dot product, with each
permitted source's key vector; those comparisons become the attention
weights. What is transferred is a weighted sum of the sources' value
vectors, which are a separate learned transformation of the same
incoming representations (§2–§3).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>If a source position has attention weight 0.804, what does the
destination receive from it?</summary>
0.804 times that source's value vector, added to the contributions of
the other permitted sources. The weight is a multiplier; the value
vector is the content being combined (§3, §5).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>During training the whole sequence is available. Why does the
model at position $i$ not use the tokens after $i$?</summary>
Because causal masking sets the scores for later positions to an
effectively infinitely negative value before softmax, giving them zero
weight. The prediction at position $i$ is then computed from positions
$1$ to $i$ only, as it will be at generation time (§4).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Is self-attention the same thing as a transformer?</summary>
No. Self-attention is one mechanism inside each transformer block. The
block also contains a feed-forward sublayer that computes on each
position separately, plus residual connections and normalization, and
the model stacks many blocks (§7).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>A model has 32 heads per layer. Does each head have a fixed,
nameable job?</summary>
Not in general. Multiple heads allow several attention patterns to run in
parallel over the same positions, but no stable, human-readable role is
assigned to any head by the architecture or the training objective, so
none should be assumed without separate evidence (§6).
</details>
:::

## 11. Continue learning

- **Vaswani et al., *Attention Is All You Need*** (paper, arXiv:1706.03762;
  Section 3.2 for attention and Sections 3.1 and 3.3 for the block are
  three pages). Technical level. The primary source for every equation on
  this page, including the multi-head construction and the reason for the
  $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling. Limitation: an encoder-decoder translation model;
  the causal decoder form used by language models is described only
  briefly, in Section 3.2.3.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>

- **3Blue1Brown, *Attention in transformers, step-by-step*** (video
  lesson, chapter 6 of the *Deep Learning* series). Introductory/visual
  level. Especially good for seeing the query, key, and value
  transformations and the weighted combination animated on actual
  vectors. Limitation: uses the "what is the token looking for" reading
  more freely than this page does; keep §2's caution in mind.
  <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/attention>

See `resources.qmd` for the complete list of sources used across this
course, with full source-map entries.
